slides: Welcome back. Today we start a new topic in geometry, similarity.

slides.say: We left it for almost the end, and that's on purpose.

slides: Similarity shows up in every shape we've learned. In triangles, in quadrilaterals, in polygons and in circles.
So first we had to learn all those shapes. Only now can we talk about similarity.

slides.say: So first, what is similarity? Here's a triangle.
Now let's copy it, exactly as it is. The copy has the same shape and the same size. Two shapes like this are called congruent.
Now let's take the same triangle and make it bigger. It's the same shape, just in another size. Two shapes like this are called similar.
So similar means the same shape, but not necessarily the same size. One shape is an enlarged copy of the other.
And here's a shape that is not similar. We stretched the triangle only sideways. It got wider, but not taller, so it's not the same shape anymore.
at: We stretched the triangle only sideways

slides.say: Now, the linear ratio. To understand it, we first need matching lines.
Matching lines are lines of the same kind, one in each shape. Let's see it with two circles.
Two circles really are similar. A small circle and a big circle have the same shape.
Take the radius of the small circle. Its matching line is the radius of the big circle. And the circumference matches the circumference.
at: Its matching line is the radius

slides.say: What we can't do is compare a diameter in one circle with a chord in the other. They're not the same kind of line.
So the linear ratio is the ratio between two matching lines.
Here are two similar triangles. I took the small one and enlarged it.
The base of the small triangle is four. The matching base in the big one is six. They match, because it's the same side of the triangle.
at: The base of the small triangle

slides: For now we just look. Soon we'll learn how to know exactly what matches what.

slides.say: So the linear ratio, from small to big, is four to six. Both numbers divide by two, so it's two to three.
at: from small to big, is four to six

slides.say: Six is four, plus half of four. So the big triangle is one and a half times the small one.
at: So the big triangle is one and a half

slides: And here's the important part. This ratio is the same for every pair of matching lines.

slides.say: We don't know the other sides. But if this side is eight, its partner is eight plus half of eight, twelve. If this side is two, its partner is three.
at: its partner is eight plus half

slides.say: Why is it always the same ratio? Because the big triangle is an enlarged copy. Every line in it was multiplied by the same number, one and a half.
Now look at the angles. The angles of the two triangles don't change.

slides: The angle on the left of the base is the same in both triangles. So is the angle on the right of the base, and so is the top angle.

slides.say: So when we enlarge a shape, the lengths grow, but the angles stay the same. We'll use this a lot with similar triangles. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
